No match. If you are unsure, call your vet.
Suspect poisoning? Contact a vet at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
Theobromine and caffeine overstimulate the heart and nerves — vomiting, restlessness, tremors, seizures.
Go to a vet immediately and bring the wrapper so the dose can be estimated.
Damages red blood cells and can cause anaemia; signs may take a day or two to appear.
Call your vet; do not induce vomiting unless a vet tells you to.
Like onion, it harms red blood cells — even small amounts are risky for dogs and cats.
Contact a vet and watch for weakness, pale gums or dark urine.
Can trigger sudden kidney failure; vomiting and lethargy are early signs.
Treat as an emergency — kidney damage can progress within hours.
Causes a sharp drop in blood sugar and can damage the liver; even one piece is dangerous.
Emergency vet visit now — this is one of the fastest-acting poisons.
Contains persin, which can upset the stomach; the stone is also a choking and blockage risk.
Call a vet if a large amount or the stone was swallowed.
Depresses the nervous system — staggering, vomiting, low body temperature, coma.
Emergency vet immediately; even small amounts are serious for pets.
Causes restlessness, a racing heart, tremors and, in large amounts, seizures.
Call a vet and keep coffee, tea, cola and energy drinks out of reach.
Cause weakness, tremors and fever in dogs, usually within 12 hours.
Call your vet; most dogs recover with supportive care.
Most pets are lactose intolerant — vomiting, diarrhoea and gas after milk or cheese.
Avoid dairy; if a large amount was eaten, offer water and call a vet.
Can splinter and cause choking, gut blockage or cracked teeth.
Do not give bones; call a vet if your pet is gagging or in pain.
Too much salt causes dehydration, tremors, seizures and, rarely, death.
Give fresh water and call a vet if a large amount was eaten.
The essential oils irritate the stomach — drooling, vomiting and diarrhoea.
Small amounts are usually mild; call a vet if signs are strong or persist.
Fresh flesh can upset the stomach; coconut water is high in potassium.
Small pieces of flesh are usually fine; avoid the water and call a vet if unwell.
Dough rises inside the stomach and produces alcohol — bloat and alcohol poisoning.
Emergency vet visit; do not wait for signs to appear.
Xylitol-based sweeteners in gum, candy and baked goods cause rapid poisoning.
Emergency vet visit now — check labels for xylitol.
Contains myristicin, which can cause disorientation, tremors and a fast heart rate.
Call a vet; keep spice jars closed and out of reach.
Cooked bones splinter easily and can pierce the gut or block the bowel.
Call a vet immediately if a cooked bone was swallowed.

Practical help for pet parents facing society, landlord or neighbour objections.
No central law bans keeping a pet in your own home. Keeping a companion animal is lawful in India.
Society bye-laws cannot take away a resident\'s right to keep a pet; they can only regulate how common areas are used.
Pets are members of the family. Wilfully harming or abandoning an animal is punishable under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960.
A resident cannot be forced to give up a pet only because another resident objects; a real, proven nuisance must be shown.
Keep your records ready: vaccination certificate, registration or licence, and any adoption or purchase proof.
If the society insists, put your request in writing and ask for the rule or bye-law in writing too. Stay calm and escalate only if needed.
Copy or share these and fill in the parts in brackets.
1. Polite request to the society or landlord

Dear Sir/Madam,

I am a resident of [Flat No. / House Name]. I would like to inform you that I keep a pet dog or cat at my home. The animal is vaccinated, registered and well looked after, and is a member of my family.

I request you to kindly note this and permit me to continue keeping my pet. I assure you that I will keep the pet clean and quiet, within my own premises, and will use the lift and common areas responsibly.

Thank you for your understanding.

Yours sincerely,
[Your Name]
[Flat No. / Contact Number]

Dear Sir/Madam,

Thank you for sharing your concern about my pet. I take it seriously and would like to clarify the following:

1. My pet is vaccinated, dewormed and registered. The records are available on request.
2. My pet does not attack or trouble anyone and is always supervised in common areas.
3. There is no central law that bans keeping a pet in a home, and society bye-laws cannot take away a resident's right to keep a pet.

I request that we resolve this amicably. I am willing to take reasonable steps such as keeping the pet leashed in common areas, avoiding peak hours in the lift, and cleaning up after it.

Yours sincerely,
[Your Name]
[Flat No. / Contact Number]

Hello, I stay in [Flat No.]. I keep a pet dog or cat at home. It is vaccinated and registered, and I always keep it clean and supervised. Please let me know if there is any specific concern and I will address it right away. Thank you.
Register or license your pet with the local body if your area requires it, and keep the certificate handy.
Maintain up-to-date vaccination and deworming records, and share them if the society asks.
Clean up after your pet in lifts, corridors and common areas, and keep your own premises clean.
Control noise: train your pet not to bark at night, and use toys or walks to reduce stress.
Use common areas responsibly: keep the pet leashed, avoid peak hours, and never leave it unattended.
Be a good neighbour: talk to residents politely, join society meetings, and offer reasonable adjustments.
This is general information, not legal advice. For a specific dispute, consult a lawyer or a local animal welfare organisation.
